messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 52
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: HVAC Technician
- Trauma Type: Toxic chemical exposure
- Pcl5: 73

**Patient Vignette: Mr. K.**

Mr. K. is a 52-year-old married man of South Eastern Asian descent who works as an HVAC technician. He presents for the first time at the urging of his wife, who has grown increasingly concerned about his withdrawal and irritability over the past eighteen months.

The traumatic event occurred in the late spring of the previous year. Mr. K. was called to a large commercial building to repair a malfunctioning chiller unit in a basement mechanical room. He recalls the air being heavy and smelling sweet, almost like rotting fruit. He was not provided with a respirator for the job, only standard gloves and safety glasses. Midway through the repair, a valve he was adjusting unexpectedly gave way, releasing a concentrated burst of refrigerant and a chemical byproduct—later identified as phosgene gas, a byproduct of heated refrigerant breakdown. He inhaled deeply before he could react, feeling a searing, chemical burn in his throat and lungs. He stumbled out of the room, coughing violently, his eyes streaming. He was taken to an emergency room, treated for acute chemical pneumonitis, and released after two days. Physical tests eventually cleared his lungs, but Mr. K. says he has never felt the same.

In the months following, Mr. K. began to avoid his work. He cannot enter a boiler room or a mechanical closet without his heart pounding. He describes the feeling as a "shaking inside" that starts in his stomach and moves up to his chest, making it hard to breathe. He has taken to refusing jobs that involve basement work or confined spaces, a pattern his employer has begun to notice with frustration. He finds excuses to send his younger apprentice into spaces he once entered without thought. The smell of any chemical—cleaning products, gasoline, even strong perfume—triggers a visceral response. He will stop mid-sentence, his face going pale, and he has to step outside. He now carries a small, portable fan in his truck to blow air on his face, a ritual he performs before every service call.

Sleep is a battleground. Mr. K. cannot fall asleep without the television on, and even then, he wakes three or four times a night. The nightmares are not replays of the explosion, but rather variations: he is trapped in a shrinking metal box, or drowning in a thick, sweet liquid. He often wakes gasping, convinced he cannot get air, and will walk through the house checking the vents and windows. He has become hypervigilant about air quality, buying three different air purifiers for his home and checking the weather report for pollution levels before he will allow his wife to open the windows.

His wife describes him as a "ghost" of the man she married. He was once a man who loved to cook elaborate Southeast Asian dishes, filling the house with the smells of lemongrass, ginger, and chili. Now, he avoids the kitchen when she cooks, saying the steam and the heat make him feel "closed in." He has stopped attending their weekly mahjong games with friends, claiming he is tired, but privately, he admits the noise and the closeness of the room make him feel trapped and panicked. He feels a profound shame about this. He was the provider, the fixer, the one who could handle anything. Now, he feels fragile, broken by something invisible.

He does not connect his current state to the event. He says, "The doctors said my lungs are fine. So why do I feel like I'm dying all the time?" He is frustrated by his own body, interpreting his symptoms as a sign of weakness or a failing of character. He spends his days in a state of low-grade dread, waiting for the next trigger, the next wave of suffocating panic. He feels disconnected from his life, watching himself go through the motions, but no longer feeling present in his own home or his own skin. The man who once fixed the air for a living is now a prisoner of it.
